newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-CBA SETS BUY-BACK, WARNS ON COSTS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CBA SETS BUY-BACK, WARNS ON COSTS.

text.p: Australia's biggest home lender Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) announced an 8 percent rise in annual profits on Wednesday, but warned of margin and cost pressures as the fallout from a home mortgage price war hits.

CBA managing director David Murray said the current 1997/98 year would be a very testing one for profits as the lagged effect of a 120 basis point squeeze in home loan margins rolled through to the bank's bottom line.

"There's a hangover effect from the reduction in home loan margins and we're making further investments for our financial services integration which will reflect in operating expenses," Murray told a news conference.

"We still have labour unit costs rising, so taken overall, it's going to be a very difficult year to make significant gains, with margin pressure and with some ongoing investments which we think are pretty good for the future," he said when asked about the profit outlook.
CBA's net profit after tax, but before abnormals, rose eight percent to A$1.206 billion, just above the median forecast by analysts of a profit of A$1.189 billion.
Net profit after abnormals fell four percent, however, to A$1.078 billion after an abnormal post-tax loss of A$128 million for a planned technology restructuring.
CBA increased its final dividend to 57 cents from 52 cents.

But the results included an increase in CBA's cost-to-income ratio in the second half to 62 percent from 60 percent in the first half and net interest margin fell to 3.41 percent from 4.00 percent over the year.
Higher wages and more than A$100 million in costs to fix the Year 2000 Millennium Bug would add to the pressure on the bank's costs in the coming year, Murray added.
Bad and doubtful debt expenses were also set to rise again as the debt cycle appeared to have troughed.
"We are running out of some fairly juicy write-back opportunities that we've had over the last few years and I really do think this year that it might have hit rock bottom."
CBA's charge for bad and doubtful debts fell to A$98 million in 1996/97 from A$113 million a year earlier.
Offsetting the warnings on future profits, CBA announced a A$650 million share buy-back to be carried out later this year to return excess capital.
Murray said the bank would still be in a strong capital position after the buy-back, with a tier one risk-adjusted capital ratio of about 7.9 percent.
With a long-term tier one target of about 7.0 percent, he said the prospects for more capital returns depended on the bank's appetite for expanding investment.
CBA also announced the formation of a partnership with U.S. information technology (IT) group Electronic Data Systems Corp to cut costs and improve its systems.
CBA said it would take a 35 percent stake in EDS Australia and that the alliance was expected to have a life of at least 10 years and generate revenues in excess of A$5 billion.
"The proposed partnership will be one of the world's largest IT (information technology) alliances within the financial services industry," CBA said.
Murray said the details on expected cost savings to flow from the alliance and the price of the 35 percent stake had yet to be finalised.
All IT functions are to be included in the partnership.
CBA's shares were down 12 cents at A$16.25 at 3.00 p.m. (0500 GMT) in a weak market overall.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
